claim: Parhyale hawaiensis is a direct developer with a body plan specified during 10 days of embryogenesis.
source: Parhyale is a direct developer; its body plan is specified during the 10 days of embryogenesis when imaging is readily possible (Browne et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Browne et al., 2005

claim: Each Parhyale embryo develops a variety of specialized appendages along the anterior-posterior axis that differ in size, shape and pattern.
source: Each embryo develops a variety of specialized appendages along the anterior-posterior axis that differ in size, shape and pattern (Martin et al., 2016; Pavlopoulos et al., 2009; Wolff and Scholtz, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martin et al., 2016; Pavlopoulos et al., 2009; Wolff and Scholtz, 2008

claim: Parhyale eggs are 500 µm long.
source: Parhyale eggs have good size and optical properties for microscopic live imaging at cellular resolution; the eggshell is transparent and embryos are 500 µm long with low autofluorescence and light scattering.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement in the manuscript

claim: Parhyale eggs have transparent eggshells.
source: Parhyale eggs have good size and optical properties for microscopic live imaging at cellular resolution; the eggshell is transparent and embryos are 500 µm long with low autofluorescence and light scattering.
evidence: Direct statement of observation in the manuscript

claim: Parhyale embryos have low autofluorescence and light scattering.
source: Parhyale eggs have good size and optical properties for microscopic live imaging at cellular resolution; the eggshell is transparent and embryos are 500 µm long with low autofluorescence and light scattering.
evidence: Direct statement of observation in the manuscript

claim: Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy (LSFM) is an ideal technology for studying how cells form tissues and organs in intact developing embryos.
source: LSFM is an ideal technology for studying how cells form tissues and organs in intact developing embryos (Huisken et al., 2004; Keller et al., 2008; Truong et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huisken et al., 2004; Keller et al., 2008; Truong et al., 2011

claim: LSFM enables biologists to capture fast and dynamic processes at very high spatiotemporal resolution, over long periods of time, and with minimal bleaching and photo-damage.
source: It enables biologists to capture fast and dynamic processes at very high spatiotemporal resolution, over long periods of time, and with minimal bleaching and photo-damage (Combs and Shroff, 2017; Huisken and Stainier, 2009; Khairy and Keller, 2011; Schmied et al., 2014; Weber et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Combs and Shroff, 2017; Huisken and Stainier, 2009; Khairy and Keller, 2011; Schmied et al., 2014; Weber et al., 2014

claim: Multi-view LSFM allows samples to be optically sectioned from multiple angles that can be combined computationally to reconstruct the entire specimen with more isotropic resolution.
source: In addition, samples can be optically sectioned from multiple angles (multi-view LSFM) that can be combined computationally to reconstruct the entire specimen with more isotropic resolution (Chhetri et al., 2015; Krzic et al., 2012; Schmid et al., 2013; Swoger et al., 2007; Tomer et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chhetri et al., 2015; Krzic et al., 2012; Schmid et al., 2013; Swoger et al., 2007; Tomer et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2013

claim: Software solutions exist for registration of acquired views, fusion of raw views into a single output z-stack, and visualization of the raw and fused images.
source: Software solutions exist for registration of acquired views, fusion of raw views (z-stacks) into a single output z-stack, and visualization of the raw and fused images (Chhetri et al., 2015; Ingaramo et al., 2014; Pietzsch et al., 2015; Preibisch et al., 2014; Preibisch et al., 2010; Rubio-Guivernau et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chhetri et al., 2015; Ingaramo et al., 2014; Pietzsch et al., 2015; Preibisch et al., 2014; Preibisch et al., 2010; Rubio-Guivernau et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016

claim: Automated approaches for cell segmentation and tracking do not yet reach the precision required for unsupervised extraction of cell lineages.
source: Automated approaches for cell segmentation and tracking have also been developed (Amat et al., 2014; Du et al., 2014; Dufour et al., 2017; Faure et al., 2016; Schiegg et al., 2015; Stegmaier et al., 2016; Ulman et al., 2017), however they do not yet reach the precision required for unsupervised extraction of cell lineages.
evidence: Supported by citations to Amat et al., 2014; Du et al., 2014; Dufour et al., 2017; Faure et al., 2016; Schiegg et al., 2015; Stegmaier et al., 2016; Ulman et al., 2017 and direct statement

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, the leg and wing primordia become progressively subdivided into distinct cell populations along the anterior-posterior (AP) and dorsal-ventral (DV) axes.
source: As revealed by lineage tracing experiments in the leading arthropod model Drosophila melanogaster, the leg and wing primordia become progressively subdivided into distinct cell populations (called compartments when lineage-restricted) along the anterior-posterior (AP) and dorsal-ventral (DV) axes (Dahmann et al., 2011; Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973; Steiner, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dahmann et al., 2011; Garcia-Bellido et al., 1973; Steiner, 1976

claim: In Drosophila, Dpp signaling controls dorsal cell fate in the leg and growth via cell proliferation in the wing.
source: In Drosophila, Dpp signaling controls dorsal cell fate in the leg and growth via cell proliferation in the wing (Barrio and Milán, 2017; Bosch et al., 2017; Brook and Cohen, 1996; Matsuda and Affolter, 2017; Rogulja and Irvine, 2005; Svendsen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrio and Milán, 2017; Bosch et al., 2017; Brook and Cohen, 1996; Matsuda and Affolter, 2017; Rogulja and Irvine, 2005; Svendsen et al., 2015

claim: Oriented cell divisions have been implicated as a general mechanism in shaping the Drosophila wing and other growing organs.
source: Besides regionalization mechanisms, oriented cell divisions have been implicated as a general mechanism in shaping the Drosophila wing and other growing organs (Baena-López et al., 2005; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baena-López et al., 2005; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013

claim: Transgenic Parhyale embryos with fluorescently labeled nuclei can be imaged routinely for several consecutive days using Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy.
source: We demonstrate here that transgenic embryos with fluorescently labeled nuclei can be imaged routinely for several consecutive days using Light-sheet Fluorescence Microscopy (LSFM).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results in the manuscript

claim: A typical 4 to 5 day long LSFM recording of Parhyale embryos was composed of more than 1 million images resulting in >7 TB datasets.
source: A typical 4 to 5 day long recording was composed of more than 1 million images resulting in >7 TB datasets.
evidence: Direct statement of data characteristics in the manuscript

claim: The relatively slow tempo of Parhyale development enabled imaging of each embryo from multiple highly overlapping views with minimal displacement of nuclei between views acquired in each time-point.
source: The relatively slow tempo of Parhyale development enabled imaging of each embryo from multiple highly overlapping views with minimal displacement of nuclei between views acquired in each time-point (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 1A showing multi-view imaging setup

claim: Segment formation and maturation in Parhyale occurred sequentially in anterior-posterior progression.
source: Segment formation and maturation in Parhyale occurred sequentially in AP progression (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 1—video 2

claim: Appendage morphogenesis in Parhyale involved patterning, growth and differentiation of ectodermal cells organized in an epithelial monolayer that gave rise to the appendage epidermis.
source: Appendage morphogenesis involved patterning, growth and differentiation of ectodermal cells organized in an epithelial monolayer that gave rise to the appendage epidermis.
evidence: Direct statement of observation in the manuscript

claim: Parhyale limbs were specified at about 3.5 days after egg-lay at 25°C.
source: In our LSFM recordings, we were particularly interested in imaging the limbs in the anterior thorax of Parhyale embryos that were specified at about 3.5 days after egg-lay (AEL) at 25˚C.
evidence: Direct statement of timing in the manuscript

claim: Over 4 days following limb specification, Parhyale limb buds bulged out ventrally, elongated along their proximal-distal axis and became progressively segmented until they acquired their definite morphology at around 8 days AEL.
source: Over the next 4 days, limb buds bulged out ventrally, elongated along their PD axis and became progressively segmented until they acquired their definite morphology at around 8 days AEL (Figure 1C–K and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 1C–K and Figure 1—video 2

claim: During germband formation, the ectoderm contributing to the posterior head and trunk of Parhyale became organized in a stereotyped grid-like pattern with ordered AP rows and DV columns of cells.
source: During germband formation, the ectoderm contributing to the posterior head and the trunk became organized in a stereotyped grid-like pattern with ordered AP rows and DV columns of cells (Figure 2A–A'') (Browne et al., 2005; Dohle et al., 2004; Dohle and Scholtz, 1988; Gerberding et al., 2002; Scholtz, 1990; Wolff and Gerberding, 2015).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 2A–A'' and citations to Browne et al., 2005; Dohle et al., 2004; Dohle and Scholtz, 1988; Gerberding et al., 2002; Scholtz, 1990; Wolff and Gerberding, 2015

claim: Each row of cells in the Parhyale germband corresponded to one parasegment.
source: Each row of cells corresponded to one parasegment, which is the unit of early metameric organization in Parhyale embryos, like in Drosophila and other arthropods (Hejnol and Scholtz, 2004; Scholtz et al., 1994).
evidence: Direct statement supported by citations to Hejnol and Scholtz, 2004; Scholtz et al., 1994

claim: Two rounds of longitudinally-oriented cell divisions in each formed parasegmental row, together with the progressive addition of new parasegments at the posterior end, led to Parhyale embryo axial elongation.
source: Two rounds of longitudinally-oriented cell divisions in each formed parasegmental row (Figure 2B–D'), together with the progressive addition of new parasegments at the posterior end, led to embryo axial elongation (Figure 1C–H).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 2B–D' and Figure 1C–H

claim: MaMuT is a hybrid and extension of two existing Fiji plugins: the BigDataViewer visualization engine and the TrackMate annotation engine.
source: This tool was dubbed MaMuT for Massive Multi-view Tracker (Figure 3) and is a hybrid and extension of two existing Fiji plugins: the BigDataViewer visualization engine (Pietzsch et al., 2015) and the TrackMate annotation engine (Tinevez et al., 2017).
evidence: Direct statement supported by citations to Pietzsch et al., 2015 and Tinevez et al., 2017

claim: MaMuT can be installed through the Fiji updater.
source: MaMuT can be installed through the Fiji updater and is tightly integrated with the other Fiji plugins for LSFM data processing.
evidence: Direct statement about software availability

claim: The source code for MaMuT is available on GitHub.
source: The source code for MaMuT is available on GitHub (Tinevez et al., 2018; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/MaMuT) and detailed tutorials and training datasets can be found at http://imagej.net/MaMuT.
evidence: Direct statement about software availability with citation to Tinevez et al., 2018

claim: In accordance with previous studies in malacostracan crustaceans and other arthropods, each Parhyale thoracic limb consisted of cells from two neighboring parasegments.
source: In accordance with previous studies in malacostracan crustaceans and other arthropods, our reconstructions demonstrated that each Parhyale thoracic limb consisted of cells from two neighboring parasegments (Browne et al., 2005; Dohle et al., 2004; Dohle and Scholtz, 1988; Hejnol and Scholtz, 2004; Scholtz, 1990; Scholtz et al., 1994; Wolff and Scholtz, 2008).
evidence: Direct statement supported by citations to Browne et al., 2005; Dohle et al., 2004; Dohle and Scholtz, 1988; Hejnol and Scholtz, 2004; Scholtz, 1990; Scholtz et al., 1994; Wolff and Scholtz, 2008

claim: The T2 limb (limb#1) developed from rows b, c and d of the E4 parasegment and from rows a and b of the E5 parasegment.
source: The T2 limb (referred to as limb#1) that we analyzed in-depth (Figure 4A–E) developed from rows b, c and d of the E4 parasegment and from rows a and b of the following E5 parasegment (Figure 4F–J').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4A–E and Figure 4F–J'

claim: Cells that arose from rows c, d and a occupied the entire length of the limb and body wall parts of the T2 segment.
source: Cells that arose from rows c, d and a occupied the entire length of the limb and body wall parts of the T2 segment, while rows b contributed only to the proximal limb and intersegmental territories (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O'

claim: 34 founder cells constituting the limb#1 primordium were fully tracked over 50 hr of development, giving rise to a total of 361 epidermal cells.
source: We fully tracked 34 founder cells constituting the limb#1 primordium over 50 hr of development, giving rise to a total of 361 epidermal cells (Figure 5 and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Direct statement of tracking results supported by Figure 5 and Figure 5—video 1

claim: The number of differential divisions observed during 50 hr varied dramatically between cells from just 1 DD in the slowest dividing lateral cells to 5 DDs in the fastest dividing central cells.
source: The number of DDs observed during these 50 hr varied dramatically between cells from just 1 DD in the slowest dividing lateral cells of the primordium (cells E4b8, E5a9/b9) to 5 DDs in the fastest dividing central cells (cells E4c3-c6 and E4d3-d6).
evidence: Direct statement of quantitative results from tracking data

claim: The reconstruction of limb#1 is the most comprehensive lineage tree for any developing arthropod limb published to date.
source: Although the clonal composition of crustacean appendages had been described previously with lipophilic dye injections (Wolff and Scholtz, 2008), the reconstruction presented here is the most comprehensive lineage tree for any developing arthropod limb published to date (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement comparing to previous work with citation to Wolff and Scholtz, 2008 and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: During limb specification and outgrowth there was a straight clonal boundary running between the anterior cells derived from the E4b, c and d rows and the posterior cells derived from the E5a and b rows.
source: In agreement with this AP restriction, during limb specification and outgrowth there was a straight clonal boundary running between the anterior cells derived from the E4b, c and d rows and the posterior cells derived from the E5a and b rows (Figure 4F–J' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4F–J' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–O'

claim: A DV separation took place at the 4-row-parasegment, running between the E4b and c rows anteriorly, between the E5a and b rows posteriorly, and between cells E4c4-c5, E4d3-d4 and E5a4-a5 medially.
source: This analysis suggested that there is indeed a DV separation that took place at the 4-row-parasegment. The DV boundary ran between the E4b and c rows anteriorly, between the E5a and b rows posteriorly, and between cells E4c4-c5, E4d3-d4 and E5a4-a5 medially (Figure 4F).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results supported by Figure 4F

claim: Throughout limb#1 development, the dorsal and ventral cells formed a sharp boundary between themselves extending along the PD axis.
source: Throughout limb#1 development, the dorsal and ventral cells formed a sharp boundary between themselves extending along the PD axis (Figure 4F–J').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4F–J'

claim: Four identical compartments (anterior-dorsal, anterior-ventral, posterior-dorsal and posterior-ventral) could be derived in limb#2 with straight boundaries and no cell mixing between neighboring compartments.
source: Four identical compartments (anterior-dorsal, anterior-ventral, posterior-dorsal and posterior-ventral) could be derived in this independent reconstruction with straight boundaries and no cell mixing between neighboring compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–H').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–H'

claim: The second mitotic wave creating the 4-row-parasegment propagated from anterior to posterior rows and from medial to lateral columns.
source: Analysis of the birth sequence of the founder cells in the two reconstructed T2 limbs largely confirmed that the second mitotic wave creating the 4-row-parasegment propagated from anterior to posterior rows and from medial to lateral columns (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results supported by Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—source data 1

claim: Division of the posterior cd cells within the 2-row-parasegment was slightly more advanced temporally compared to their anterior ab sister cells.
source: First, as previously noted (Scholtz, 1990), division of the posterior cd cells within the 2-row-parasegment was slightly more advanced temporally compared to their anterior ab sister cells (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5A–C and citation to Scholtz, 1990

claim: The temporal sequence of divisions exhibited a certain degree of variability between the two analyzed limbs.
source: Second, the temporal sequence of divisions, which gave rise to a stereotyped number and spatial arrangement of the 34 founder cells in each primordium, exhibited a certain degree of variability between the two analyzed limbs; for example, division of the E4cd8/9 cells preceded division of E4cd7 in limb#1 but not in lim#2, whereas division of the E4cd6/7 cells preceded division of E4cd5 in limb#2 but not in limb#1 (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Direct statement of comparative analysis supported by Figure 5A–B

claim: It was possible to register the two growth curves during the period when all cells were tracked faithfully by applying a linear temporal rescaling factor of 1.6.
source: Yet, it was possible to register the two growth curves during the period when all cells were tracked faithfully by applying a linear temporal rescaling factor of 1.6, effectively correcting for the temperature-induced change in growth (Figure 5D).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis method supported by Figure 5D

claim: After temporal alignment, the increase in cell number was very similar between developing limbs, up to 35 hr after the first tracked division.
source: After this temporal alignment, the increase in cell number was very similar between developing limbs, up to 35 hr after the first tracked division.
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results

claim: The first step in limb bud formation was the rise of few cells at the intersection of the four compartments above the level of the germband at around 96 hr AEL.
source: At the cellular level, the first step in this transformation was the rise of few cells at the intersection of the four compartments above the level of the germband at around 96 hr AEL (Figure 4G,G' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F,F').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4G,G' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F,F'

claim: Within 3 hr following the initial rise of cells, this initial phase was followed by a large-scale elevation of most cells in the dorsal compartment.
source: Within the following 3 hr, this initial phase was followed by a large-scale elevation of most cells in the dorsal compartment.
evidence: Direct statement of observation

claim: The intersection of the AP and DV boundaries was at the tip of the limb bud and persisted in this position throughout subsequent elongation.
source: The intersection of the AP and DV boundaries was at the tip of the limb bud and persisted in this position throughout subsequent elongation (Figure 4H–J' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–H').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4H–J' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–H'

claim: From 103 hr AEL onwards, a second element appeared bulging distally off the original bud in limb#1.
source: From 103 hr AEL onwards, a second element appeared bulging distally off the original bud in limb#1 (Figure 4I,I').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4I,I'

claim: The limb elongated as a convoluted rather than straight cylinder and acquired progressively an S-shape.
source: The limb elongated as a convoluted rather than straight cylinder and acquired progressively an S-shape (Figure 4J,J').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4J,J'

claim: There was a striking difference in cell cycle length between central cells that were dividing faster than their neighbors in the periphery of the primordium (average CCL 7.1–8.5 hr versus 8.5–16.4 hr, respectively).
source: This quantification revealed a striking difference in CCL between central cells that were dividing faster than their neighbors in the periphery of the primordium (average CCL 7.1–8.5 hr versus 8.5–16.4 hr, respectively).
evidence: Direct statement of quantitative analysis results

claim: The difference in cell cycle length started from early primordium specification at the 4-row-parasegment.
source: This difference started from early primordium specification at the 4-row-parasegment (Figure 6E), but became most pronounced during the global elevation of the limb bud (Figure 4F), suggesting a causal association between spatially controlled cell proliferation and initiation of limb outgrowth (see Discussion).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6E and Figure 4F

claim: During subsequent elongation stages, a high concentration of fast dividing cells was located at the intersection of the four presumptive compartments, resembling a growth zone at the distal tip of the growing appendage.
source: During subsequent elongation stages, a high concentration of fast dividing cells was located at the intersection of the four presumptive compartments, resembling a growth zone at the distal tip of the growing appendage (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6G,H

claim: Another row of faster dividing cells was localized in the anterior cells abutting the AP boundary.
source: Another row of faster dividing cells was localized in the anterior cells abutting the AP boundary (Figure 6H,H').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6H,H'

claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed that the 34 founder cells formed three clusters based on their division patterns.
source: This analysis revealed very similar profiles in the two limbs, as well as their average, with their cells forming three clusters (Figure 7A–C and Figure 7—source data 1): the first cluster contained cells E4c3-c7 and E4d3-d7 displaying the fastest proliferation rates and giving rise to most of the limb structures; the second cluster contained the majority of E4 and E5 b cells corresponding to the slowest dividing cells of ventral fate and contributing to the proximal limb and intersegmental territories; the third cluster contained the remaining cells exhibiting mixed division patterns, including most of the posterior E5a cells and the more lateral E4c and d cells.
evidence: Direct statement of clustering analysis results supported by Figure 7A–C and Figure 7—source data 1

claim: Pairwise comparisons revealed low distances between the 34 homologous cells in limb#1 and limb#2 with a median difference of 19.3%.
source: Pairwise comparisons revealed low distances between the 34 homologous cells in limb#1 and limb#2 with a median difference of 19.3% (Figure 7D).
evidence: Direct statement of quantitative comparison supported by Figure 7D

claim: The distribution of distances between homologous cells was significantly shifted towards lower values relative to pairwise comparisons between non-homologous cells across the two limbs.
source: The distribution of these distances between homologous cells was significantly shifted towards lower values relative to pairwise comparisons between non-homologous cells across the two limbs (Figure 7D and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison supported by Figure 7D and Figure 7—source data 1

claim: All early divisions in the limb#1 primordium were parallel to the AP axis confirming the strict longitudinal orientation of row divisions.
source: All early divisions in the limb#1 primordium were parallel to the AP axis confirming the strict longitudinal orientation of row divisions (Figure 8F).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 8F

claim: Cell divisions acquired a more heterogeneous pattern after the 4-row-parasegment.
source: Cell divisions acquired a more heterogeneous pattern after the 4-row-parasegment (Figure 8G).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 8G

claim: An increasing number of mitotic spindles aligned progressively along the PD axis during limb bud formation and elongation.
source: An increasing number of mitotic spindles aligned progressively along the PD axis during limb bud formation (Figure 8H) and elongation (Figure 8I,J).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 8H, Figure 8I, and Figure 8J

claim: Parhyale limb outgrowth is driven by at least two patterned cell behaviors: the differential rates of cell proliferation and the orderly arrangement of mitotic spindles.
source: Collectively, the information extracted from our spatiotemporally resolved lineage trees strongly suggested that Parhyale limb outgrowth is driven by at least two patterned cell behaviors: the differential rates of cell proliferation and the orderly arrangement of mitotic spindles.
evidence: Direct statement of inference from data analysis

claim: The cells that gave rise to the proximal, medial and distal limb segments occupied distinct mediolateral positions in the germband grid at the 4-row-parasegment and distinct PD positions in the early limb bud.
source: This analysis showed that the cells that gave rise to the proximal, medial and distal limb segments occupied distinct mediolateral positions in the germband grid at the 4-row-parasegment (Figure 9M) and distinct PD positions in the early limb bud (Figure 9N).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 9M and Figure 9N

claim: When the limb bud split into two elements, the proximal element gave rise to the proximal limb segments coxa, basis and ischium, while the distal element gave rise to the distal limb segments merus, carpus, propodus, and dactylus.
source: When the limb bud split into two elements, the proximal element gave rise to the proximal limb segments coxa, basis and ischium, while the distal element gave rise to the distal limb segments merus, carpus, propodus, and dactylus (Figure 9O–R).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 9O–R

claim: The cells forming the distal segments originated as a disc of cells centered at the intersection of the four compartments with contributions from the E4c4-c6, E4d3-d6 and E5a3-a6 sublineages.
source: The cells forming the distal segments originated as a disc of cells centered at the intersection of the four compartments with contributions from the E4c4-c6, E4d3-d6 and E5a3-a6 sublineages (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: During the subsequent elongation stages, distal cells kept separate from more proximal cells at the prospective ischium/merus joint.
source: During the subsequent elongation stages, distal cells kept separate from more proximal cells at the prospective ischium/merus joint, suggesting that limb segments may pose secondary lineage restrictions along the PD axis (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) (Milán and Cohen, 2000).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and citation to Milán and Cohen, 2000

claim: The region of high/moderate Ph-dpp expression was localized to rows E4c, E4d and E5a that mostly contribute to the presumptive dorsal compartment.
source: Acknowledging that the graded Ph-dpp expression obscured the precise limits of its expression, this analysis suggested that the region of high/moderate Ph-dpp expression was localized to rows E4c, E4d and E5a that mostly contribute to the presumptive dorsal compartment, while low/no Ph-dpp expression could be detected in the prospective ventral rows E4b anteriorly and E5b posteriorly (Figure 10A'').
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results supported by Figure 10A''

claim: Ph-dpp expression faded in the medial (prospective ventral) columns and the border between high/moderate and low/no expressing cells was located in descendent cells from column 4.
source: Furthermore, Ph-dpp expression faded in the medial (prospective ventral) columns and the border between high/moderate and low/no expressing cells was located in descendent cells from column 4 as also predicted by our in silico cellular analysis (Figure 10A–A'').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10A–A''

claim: In embryos 96–108 hr AEL, the domain of strong Ph-dpp expression was more localized in the row of anterior-dorsal cells abutting the AP boundary.
source: In embryos 96–108 hr AEL, the domain of strong Ph-dpp expression was more localized in the row of anterior-dorsal cells abutting the AP boundary (Figure 10D–D'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1D,D').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10D–D'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1D,D'

claim: Expression of Ph-Doc was detected in a subset of the Ph-dpp-expressing cells at 84–96 hr AEL.
source: Expression of the single Doc gene identified in Parhyale (Ph-Doc) was detected in a subset of the Ph-dpp-expressing cells at 84–96 hr AEL (Figure 10B–B'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B,B'), while 12 hr later the two genes exhibited essentially identical strong expression in the cells abutting the AP boundary (Figure 10E–E'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1E,E').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10B–B'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B,B'

claim: 12 hr after 84-96 hr AEL, Ph-dpp and Ph-Doc exhibited essentially identical strong expression in the cells abutting the AP boundary.
source: Expression of the single Doc gene identified in Parhyale (Ph-Doc) was detected in a subset of the Ph-dpp-expressing cells at 84–96 hr AEL (Figure 10B–B'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B,B'), while 12 hr later the two genes exhibited essentially identical strong expression in the cells abutting the AP boundary (Figure 10E–E'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1E,E').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10E–E'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1E,E'

claim: Cells expressing Ph-dpp and Ph-Doc exhibited the highest rates of cell proliferation.
source: In both stages analyzed, cells expressing Ph-dpp and Ph-Doc also exhibited the highest rates of cell proliferation (compare Figure 10D'',E'' with Figure 6G,H) providing strong correlative evidence for a morphogen-dependent control of Parhyale limb growth.
evidence: Direct statement of correlation supported by comparison of Figure 10D'',E'' with Figure 6G,H

claim: Ph-H15 transcripts were detected specifically in the b row cells.
source: In agreement with these predictions, in situ hybridization analyses detected the Ph-H15 transcripts specifically in the b row cells.
evidence: Direct statement of in situ hybridization results

claim: Ph-H15 expression initiated shortly after the ab cells divided longitudinally into the a and b daughter cells in each forming 4-row-parasegment.
source: Furthermore, expression initiated shortly after the ab cells divided longitudinally into the a and b daughter cells in each forming 4-row-parasegment (Figure 10C–C'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1C,C').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10C–C'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1C,C'

claim: Although Ph-H15 was first activated in all b cells, during later divisions Ph-H15 expression faded in the more medial columns and persisted only in the ventral limb cells close to the body wall.
source: Although Ph-H15 was first activated in all b cells, during later divisions Ph-H15 expression faded in the more medial columns (Figure 10C–C'') and persisted only in the ventral limb cells close to the body wall (Figure 10F–F'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1F,F').
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 10C–C'', Figure 10F–F'' and Figure 10—figure supplement 1F,F'

claim: The MaMuT reconstruction of the Parhyale T2 limb required about 10 weeks of dedicated manual cell tracking by an experienced annotator.
source: The MaMuT reconstruction of the Parhyale T2 limb described in this article required about 10 weeks of dedicated manual cell tracking by an experienced annotator.
evidence: Direct statement of time required for manual tracking

claim: Three-day old transgenic embryos with fluorescently labeled nuclei were mounted for LSFM in low melting agarose with scattered fluorescent beads.
source: Three-day old transgenic embryos with fluorescently labeled nuclei were mounted for LSFM in low melting agarose with scattered fluorescent beads.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental method

claim: A multi-view acquisition was made every 7.5 min at 26°C.
source: A multi-view acquisition was made every 7.5 min at 26˚C.
evidence: Direct statement of imaging parameters

claim: The H2B-mRFPruby fluorescence levels were replenished regularly every 12 hr by raising the temperature in the chamber from 26°C to 37°C and heat-shocking the embryo for 1 hr.
